etymologies.etymologyHTML: Apparently from an unrecorded Middle English *gust, from Old Norse gustr (“a gust, blast”), from Proto-Germanic *gustiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-. Cognate with Icelandic gustur (“gust of wind”). Related also to Old Norse gusa (“to gush forth”), Old High German gussa (“flood”), Middle English guschen (> English gush). The English word was not recorded before Shakespeare.

definitions.definition: A strong, abrupt rush of wind.

quote.citation: 2017 August 26, Anne Marie Roantree, Venus Wu, “Battered Hong Kong and Macau brace for Pakhar, more flooding”, in Andrew Hay, editor, Reuters‎[1], archived from the original on 2023-08-05, COMMODITIES NEWS‎[2]:
quote.text: The maximum sustained winds recorded at Waglan Island, Tate’s Cairn and Cheung Chau Beach were 113, 101 and 97 kmh (70, 62, 60 mph) respectively, with maximum gusts 135, 154 and 130 kmh (84, 96, 81 mph)

definitions.definition: (by extension) Any rush or outburst (of water, emotion, etc.).

quote.citation: 1609 (revised 1625), Francis Bacon, De Sapientia Veterum ('Wisdom of the Ancients')
quote.text: they are merely driven about by every sudden gust and impulse of the mind

quote.citation: 1869 May, Anthony Trollope, “Hard Words”, in He Knew He Was Right, volume I, London: Strahan and Company, […], →OCLC, page 73:
quote.text: The author is not speaking now of actual love-makings, of intrigues and devilish villany, either perpetrated or imagined; but rather of those passing gusts of short-lived and unfounded suspicion to which, as to other accidents, very well-regulated families may occasionally be liable.

quote.citation: 2019 April 25, Samanth Subramanian, “Hand dryers v paper towels: the surprisingly dirty fight for the right to dry your hands”, in The Guardian‎[3]:
quote.text: Do the dryers disperse bacteria and viruses through the restroom, like autumn breezes gusting leaves across a lawn?

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gust, guste, from Latin gustus (“taste”) and Old French gust, goust.

quote.text: An ox will relish the tender flesh of kids with as much gust and appetite.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], (please specify |epistle=I to IV), London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Destroy all creatures for thy sport or gust.

quote.citation: 1695, C[harles] A[lphonse] du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica. The Art of Painting, […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Heptinstall for W. Rogers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A choice of it may be made according to the gust and manner of the ancients.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gusten (“to taste, have a taste for”), from the noun (see above).

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To have a relish for.
